theme: In the LORD I take refuge; save, O LORD
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 11 and Psalm 12. Both psalms respond to a world where the foundations seem to be crumbling. Notice what David says about the LORD in each.
settingTheScene: Psalm 11 was written when David’s friends were advising him to flee like a bird to the mountains. Psalm 12 laments the decline of honest speech in the community. Both are attributed to David and fit the period of Saul’s persecution, when the order of the kingdom was breaking down. They are paired here because together they address the question of what to do when righteousness seems to be losing.
observation: “In the LORD I take refuge; how can you say to my soul, Flee like a bird to your mountain” (11:1).
“If the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?” (11:3).
“The LORD is in his holy temple; the LORD’s throne is in heaven; his eyes see, his eyelids test the children of man” (11:4).
“For the LORD is righteous; he loves righteous deeds; the upright shall behold his face” (11:7).
“Save, O LORD, for the godly one is gone; for the faithful have vanished from among the children of man” (12:1).
“Everyone utters lies to his neighbor; with flattering lips and a double heart they speak” (12:2).
“Because the poor are plundered, because the needy groan, I will now arise, says the LORD; I will place him in the safety for which he longs” (12:5).
“The words of the LORD are pure words, like silver refined in a furnace on the ground, purified seven times” (12:6).
interpretation:
Psalm 11 begins with a tempting suggestion from friends: run. “The wicked bend the bow; they have fitted their arrow to the string to shoot in the dark at the upright in heart.” Things look dangerous, and the foundations of order are shaking. The question, “What can the righteous do?” is an honest one. David’s answer is not to deny the danger but to look past it: “The LORD is in his holy temple; the LORD’s throne is in heaven.” The foundations may shake, but the throne does not.

The point is that God sees. His eyes “test the children of man.” He is not absent, and he is not passive. He loves righteous deeds, and he will deal with the wicked. For those who trust him, the final promise is the best: “The upright shall behold his face.” To see God’s face is the greatest reward of the faithful.

Psalm 12 turns to a different danger: the corruption of speech. Lies, flattery, and the boasting of the proud have taken over. The godly seem to have vanished. Anyone who feels isolated in their commitment to truth will recognize the mood. David does not hide the situation, and he brings it to God.

God answers in the middle of the psalm, in his own voice. “Because the poor are plundered, because the needy groan, I will now arise.” He hears the groaning of the poor, and he acts. It is one of the most comforting words in the Psalter.

The contrast with human words is stark. The speech of men is double-hearted, but “the words of the LORD are pure words, like silver refined in a furnace.” When all speech around us is unreliable, the word of God is the one thing we can trust completely. He will keep us and guard us from this generation forever.
connection: Jesus is the truth (John 14:6), the Word who is himself pure and without deceit (1 Peter 2:22). Hebrews 12:27-28 speaks of receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken. He is in heaven now, at the right hand of the throne (Hebrews 8:1). Matthew 5:8 says, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God,” echoing Psalm 11:7. Revelation 22:4 says, “They will see his face.”
application:
When you feel the urge to flee, remember that the LORD is on his throne.

Examine your own speech this week. Where is there flattery or exaggeration in it?

Open your Bible with trust that these words are pure and reliable.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what feels shaken in your life right now.
Ask him to keep your lips from flattery and your heart undivided.
Thank him that his words are pure and trustworthy.
